proof_summary: Assuming either family is bounded by \(N\), apply the decomposition hypothesis to \((N+2)!/6\), obtaining \((N+2)!=(6x-1)+(6y+1)\) with the indicated terms prime. Boundedness makes \(6x-1\) (in the Sophie Germain case), or \(6y+1\) (in the twin-prime case), divide the factorial and hence the complementary prime; primality forces equality or a divisor of \(1\), both impossible from positivity and their distinct residues modulo \(6\).
